biur-halacha/6:_: Within his house — see what Chacham Tzvi wrote; behold even though in Or Zarua it appears his practical conclusion is like his grandfather Maharash as we will quote below, Chacham Tzvi ruled like Ateret Zekenim because that colleague came later and mentioned only his view as we wrote in Mishna Berurah in his name; nevertheless what Chacham Tzvi was more lenient than him is not clear at all; I will quote Chacham Tzvi's words: a partner of a mourner who died on chol hamoed — permitted to deal in the shop immediately after Yom Tov [Ateret Zekenim siman 548] (what Ateret Zekenim concluded "like other mourning" means like there on the seventh day permitted to open his shop — so here if he died on the first day of chol hamoed permitted immediately after Yom Tov that is the seventh day) — it appears for us who practice prohibition only three days, likewise if he died on last Yom Tov — permitted — end quote; in truth not comparable, for there the mourner sat at least three days in mourning whereas here he has not sat at all; our leniency suffices if he died on chol hamoed on the first day per Ateret Zekenim, for at least now it is the seventh day from death — not to grasp two leniencies, three days and no mourning conduct at all [especially Pri Megadim doubts Ateret Zekenim too and tends to be stringent like his grandfather; if we are lenient like Ateret Zekenim, no more]. I quote Or Zarua: it appears to me a partner of a mourner who died on chol hamoed first day — permitted to deal in the shop immediately after Yom Tov, since we are lenient in other mourning after three days; but I heard in name of my grandfather the Gaon he ruled to forbid like other mourning — end quote; behold even Ateret Zekenim's view is only three days for a partner generally, as Maharshal; nevertheless in our case he was stringent specifically if died on chol hamoed first day so opening the shop is at least on the seventh day from death, as above; therefore the reason as we wrote above is clear in my humble opinion. Know that regarding close report it is simple: although seven days from death already passed, commerce is forbidden all mourning like other mourners, Yoreh De'ah 402 — close report is like burial day; so Pri Megadim end of siman:
biur-halacha/8:א: (1) And it is permissible to wash near the evening - per the Rama's opinion that it is more serious near the evening 34 for the matter of washing DHA for the matter of telling and washing and it is appropriate in the Yora De'a sign that 26 33 in the Hagah Ai'ish. And the Rama's opinion is close to the evening. As simple as that:
biur-halacha/8:ב: (2) Vatzel if it falls, etc. - he resorted to Lishna Vatzel because when he was paid eight days before the habit, surely the Peshita Dargal cancels the ruling of thirty and it is permissible to cut a haircut on that day and it falls on the eighth day of Shabbat, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.
biur-halacha/8:ג: Permitted to cut hair on erev Shabbat — likewise to launder and wash; it appears here one need not wait until after Mincha prayer, unlike above where it must be evident it is for festival honor — unlike here:
biur-halacha/10:_: For the festival does not cancel, etc. — see Mishna Berurah that the custom is to be lenient; and therefore one whose relative died on erev Shabbat when that Shabbat is erev the festival is permitted to bathe on erev Shabbat close to dark in hot water for honor of the festival [Terumat HaDeshen siman 287, and Shach brought it in Yoreh De'ah siman 399, and Magen Avraham in our matter]; and see Avnei Nezer who challenged them, for Darkei Moshe wrote there the custom in this is to be stringent; and see Peri Megadim who is also doubtful: even though we are lenient on the eve of the festival itself for honor of the festival, there is no proof from this to be lenient also on erev Shabbat for this reason [and there is no proof from that which we are lenient when the eighth day falls on Shabbat to bathe on erev Shabbat, for there the seven days of mourning already ended]; and one may side to be lenient only in cold water on erev Shabbat, and likewise Chayei Adam leans to be stringent in this [and it is obvious that therefore even if his seventh day falls on Shabbat erev the festival, it is likewise forbidden to bathe on erev Shabbat, and so in Chacham Adam there]; however in Darkei Halacha and likewise in Noda B'Yehuda Moed Katan part Yoreh De'ah siman 99 they brought Terumat HaDeshen's words as halakha [however one may question, for it contradicts what he wrote in Bedek HaBayis to Yoreh De'ah where he answered Rama's words that he permits only in cold water, per Avnei Nezer]; the upshot: one who wishes to rely to be lenient certainly they do not protest, after Shach and Magen Avraham and Darkei Halacha brought Terumat HaDeshen as halakha; and Avnei Nezer's challenge is only from custom, for Darkei Moshe wrote there they practice to be stringent:
chokhmat-shlomo/1:_: Seif 1 — one who buries his dead during the festival, mourning does not apply on the festival, etc. NB: a case came before me where one became a mourner on Sukkot, may he read Torah on Simchat Torah? I permitted based on this: since everyone practices reading Torah, if the mourner does not read it is public; although one may distinguish — there Rabbenu Tam practiced reading in that place and it is public; but here perhaps he read elsewhere; R' Shlomo responsum 71 regarding a mourner who circumcised his son — he does not read Torah; nevertheless here another reason: since Shulchan Aruch permits a mourner on erev Yom Tov to leave for slichot, though other days forbidden — here since people increase slichot, pain if he sits home; likewise on Simchat Torah since all Israel read, pain if he sits and does not read; compare Taz Hilchot Shabbat 244 regarding attached melacha — marit ayin only when two sides to permit; if only one side to permit we fear perhaps this one knows it is not in the pot and will think he is a day laborer, etc.; so here. For one who circumcised his son there are two sides: perhaps they do not know today is milah day; if he has no milah he has no reason to read today; even if they know milah day perhaps he already read in another synagogue — therefore two sides to permit, no marit ayin concern. But on Simchat Torah since all read today and no other permit side except perhaps he read elsewhere — one may fear many know he did not read elsewhere and will recognize he refrains because of mourning — public. True one may distinguish Taz's case from ours; nevertheless at least no public concern, since rabbinic matter, especially on festival mourning does not apply; also from pain reason above one may be lenient — clear and correct for law; examine well:
chokhmat-shlomo/2:_: (There seif 5) Although mourning does not apply during the festival, onen status applies, etc., etc. — note: I was asked about a deceased on the second day of Yom Tov whom they would not allow to be buried until near evening per the king's law, may it go well with us — whether onen status applies here or not. I answered it seems obvious onen status applies here, for even though Magen Avraham wrote where it is impossible to bury because of non-Jewish dominion onen status does not apply — that is if impossible all day; but if possible to bury him today only after a time, what difference does the day make — we do not split it, and whoever will be buried today, onen status applies to him. And it is not comparable to what is established regarding a deceased on Yom Tov — that then at night he becomes impure and onen status does not apply to him — namely, also night and day the change is evident and they are separate entities, therefore onen status did not apply to him in the interim; but on the day itself, where the change is not evident, we do not split it into two. And behold some wished to bring proof from what Magen Avraham wrote above siman 526 that perhaps he holds since his intent is not to bury until after the meal, onen status did not apply to them until after the meal, see there — if so, here too. But in my opinion behold Magen Avraham's words themselves are astonishing — if there is reason to distinguish thus, what proof does the Rosh bring in chapter 3 of Berachot from the Rambam that there is no onen status on Yom Tov from that they had to bring a shofar before him to take him out on the 18th — what proof is it? Perhaps there his intent was to bury them after the meal, therefore onen status did not apply to him; but where his intent is to bury them earlier, there is onen status on Yom Tov — and perforce this view does not exist. However, even according to Magen Avraham's words it is not comparable: one, behold we see Magen Avraham was precise only if his intent is to bury after the meal — but if his intent is to bury after prayer they would be exempt from prayer, and perforce we require something else interrupting in the interim between the mitzvah and the burial — something else interrupting and the distinction evident in this, similar to day and night where at night onen status did not apply to him — so too here; but if there is no interrupting change in the interim, exempt from prayer — if so, here too, since between the hour they do not allow him to be buried and the hour they will allow him to be buried there is no evident change. For granted there, since the matter is contingent on the meal and it is a matter contingent on action and evident — therefore one may split the day itself; but between hours where the change is not evident, it is impossible to split the day itself into two. And further, granted after the meal, since this is a fixed time for all deceased and it is known that today they do not bury except after the meal — therefore there is no disgrace to the deceased, for all know it is not his burial time until after the meal; but here, per the king's law, since hours are not all equal and there is a deceased they leave to bury in the morning when his time has ended — who will know this one is not buried because his time has not ended? Therefore it is disgrace to the deceased if they engage in prayer; and behold for this reason an onen is forbidden to be stringent based on honor of the deceased — so too here disgrace of the deceased applies, therefore forbidden to pray. And it is as if they do not allow him all day to be buried — onen status does not apply there, for when the public sees they did not bury him all day, all will know it is because burial was impossible and there is no disgrace to the deceased since burial is literally another day; but on that day itself, if burial will be that day, one may say from laxity they delay him — then one may split the day itself into two where there is no fixed time for all deceased equally; therefore they certainly have onen status. And likewise if there is delay — they do not wish to allow burial until tomorrow but the onenim have ability to strive to bury him today near evening — onen status also applies in the morning. And it is not comparable to one in captivity who did not despair of burial — onen status does not apply to him, only mourning — for there he is not yet buried at all; therefore even though they can strive to bury him, since it is in doubt he has no onen status; but here it is known he will be buried tomorrow, and since he will certainly be buried tomorrow and it is also possible through striving he will be buried today, onen status applies from today. And especially there it deals with something hinging on much money and it is doubtful whether it will help — therefore onen status did not apply to them; but here with a small sum it helps and it is close to certain it will help — therefore onen status applies to them; and on the contrary it appears that because of this onen status applies from now even if they will not bury him until after the meal or after the festival ends — nevertheless from now this striving applies to them, and therefore it is like one who darkens before the boundary — onen status applies from when he begins to darken before the boundary — so too here. And this is correct for practical law that they are exempt from all mitzvot like other onenim on Yom Tov; and see clear proof to this from Magen Avraham's own words siman 496 s.k. 6 — it is proven there that even though by law burial is forbidden until after the megillah, nevertheless onen status applies and he is exempt — all the more so here, see there and examine; and even for Magen Avraham's conclusion there, it was only regarding megillah, for megillah precedes burial of the deceased as Magen Avraham wrote; and also in the book Avnei Nezer disagrees with Magen Avraham — also there; but in our case certainly he is not allowed to pray — examine well. (There) And if he died on Yom Tov and does not wish to bury him that day, onen status does not apply to him, etc. — note: from this it is clear that even if his intent is to bury at night, nevertheless there is no onen status on Yom Tov since he has no intent to bury that day — all the more so on Shabbat and Yom Kippur when burial is forbidden that day, there is no onen status. And I was very astonished from the Gemara Yoma daf 13 that asks: and R' Yehuda — even another wife they prepare for him lest his wife die — and if his wife dies in the middle of the service is he an onen, etc. — what does it ask? And what compares Yom Kippur to weekday? Behold one may say on Yom Kippur, since if possible to bury her today onen status does not apply to him — and one should not say that for onen in kodshim we do not follow whether he can bury or not — from where to challenge thus? And perhaps also for onen status in kodshim onen status applies only if he wishes to bury that day — for this is learned from the verse of Aharon 'on that very day they offered,' etc., and there burial was given that day; but without burial being given, perhaps onen status does not apply at all — why does it ask? And requires further study. And even though there is one tanna in Moed Katan that Rosh Hashana and Yom Kippur are not like festivals — nevertheless what does it ask? And let us say R' Yehuda holds like the one who says Rosh Hashana and Yom Kippur are like festivals and therefore onen status does not apply if he does not bury that day — end of the matter that it requires further study — examine. And see in my work on Orach Chayim from the year 5596 section 132 that a certain scholar named our teacher R' Eikel from the community of Botoshatsh wished to refute the above difficulty and I refuted all his words and the difficulty stands in its place — see there well. And behold when I was speaking in the sugya of Yoma there, it seems to decide from this what Taz and Shach dispute in Yoreh De'ah siman 391, and Nekudas HaKesef brought the dispute of early authorities whether mourning befell a groom after chuppah who has not yet consummated — whether mourning applies first or the seven days of festivity, see there. In my humble opinion one may prove from this: at first glance it is difficult — why does the Gemara ask that R' Yehuda said lest his wife die and if she dies he performs service — behold he is an onen, etc. — why does it ask? And perhaps where possible to fix they fix, and what is impossible they do not fix; and especially since the Gemara concludes in Sukkah that R' Yehuda was not concerned for death except based on a general virtue he was concerned for death — if so, it works for what relates to atonement for all Israel; but for what relates to prohibition of onen status and lest he eat in this we are not concerned for death — why does it ask? And one must say the Gemara understood from R' Yehuda's language that he said 'they prepare another wife for him' — perforce he married before Yom Kippur, for if on Yom Kippur there would be no need for preliminary invitation, not like the Yerushalmi — therefore it is difficult to him why he does not marry on Yom Kippur; and perforce based on rabbinic enactment one does not betroth on Shabbat and Yom Tov, and where possible to fix so he does not come to this they fix — therefore it asks: since the concern is from rabbinic enactment not to betroth, better he should not marry now — for if he marries her now perhaps his wife will die and he will be an onen; better to wait to marry her on Yom Kippur, and then since he will see he needs to die first and marry her for that — like the kind the Gemara asks there — so one may say here: since he sees he needs to die first and marry, and conditionally if the other dies and he will not have two homes — then if she dies mourning days of festivity apply retroactively and he will not become an onen again; if so, better not to be concerned for rabbinic prohibition of betrothal than now that he married beforehand and behold we require a chuppah fit for consummation. And granted on Yom Kippur the chuppah fit for consummation will be in the evening and this is considered fit for consummation as I wrote in my novellae already, see there; but if he marries beforehand, behold all seven days they separate him from his house — perforce he marries beforehand — if so, the seven days of festivity already ended before Yom Kippur, therefore he will have onen status — so goes the Gemara's difficulty, that better to be concerned for prohibition of onen status than rabbinic prohibition of betrothal — examine, for I abbreviated. And it is proven from this that even without consummation mourning days of festivity apply first and he has no onen status — for behold on Yom Kippur he will not consummate, and it asks thus — understand, for I abbreviated. And behold I reconsidered and saw this is an error for several reasons: for even though seven days of festivity override mourning, nevertheless they do not override onen status if they wish to bury that day — it is no better than Yom Tov where onen status applies if they bury that day; and one should not say behold his intent is to bury that day — this is difficult without this, as above. And further, behold betrothal without chuppah is not his home — perforce he brought her in — if so, again impossible to say conditionally, for there is no condition in chuppah; and further from either way: if he betroths her now, again if the first dies he would have service in two homes retroactively; and if he betroths her only conditionally if she dies — then if she dies onen status applies from the start and afterward festivity; and further behold the Gemara concludes his difficulty is not from onen status, only lest he be troubled — and behold this will not be fixed even if he betroths and brings her in and mourning days of festivity apply — nevertheless will he not be troubled? Who is not troubled? And behold in the end it is impossible to fix the matter — therefore let these words I wrote be omitted; and in any case the mishnah did not move from its place — mere pilpul — examine well.

In my humble opinion it seems permitted on Shabbat and Yom Tov to study Torah; and you may know from what they said in Moed Katan daf 23b: the difference between them is marital relations — he did not say Torah study; if so, by inference all agree Torah study is permitted; and perhaps Maharam of Lublin spoke only on the night of the second day of Yom Tov.

eliyah-rabbah/7:_: [7] And there is no need to comfort him, etc. Also, one should not comfort the mourner on the eve of Shabbat, after which the first leg was blessed with a kahai guona if seven days have already passed since the death of the deceased (I found it in the name of Tosaf Yom Tov), and also if there is a last Yom Tov on the eve of Shabbat, even though there are no seven days before the death of the dead (16 Rish Siman 1526), but what he wrote there was not legal. Let's do every thirtieth as the Shach wrote in sign T, and also by changing the place, even if it comes after his knee, since they do it every thirty, there is nothing in the parshasia, even if it didn't start in the sand, to change what I wrote with a brush this sign that one should not change on foot from any place on Shabbat.

eliyah-rabbah/9:_: [9] To wash and cut hair, etc. — so it is in all books of Shulchan Aruch; and what he wrote 'one need not wait until night' must be said to refer to bathing, which is permitted at night; and in this manner Beit Yosef explained the Tur's words at the beginning of daf 76 as mentioned above, and not like R' Moshe Rivkash who deletes the words 'and cut hair'; and what he wrote that it is not in Mordechai and Hagahot Ashiri — this is no difficulty, for Rama follows his reasoning in Yoreh De'ah siman 559 seif 3 that one may not cut hair close to evening; and further it appears to him they learned bathing from haircutting as Darkei Moshe wrote. Further R' Moshe wrote: what is written 'one need not wait,' etc. — meaning he may wash in cold water — up to here; and if his intent is that Rama does not allow on erev Yom Tov except in cold water, he overlooked Darkei Moshe's words in Yoreh De'ah who wrote, in the name of Terumat HaDeshen siman 287 that he allows even in hot water — we practice thus; and if his intent is on Yom Tov itself, for Rama wrote in siman 511 that we practice to forbid hot bathing — it is difficult for him what is said 'one need not wait,' for it is forbidden; therefore he explained: he may wash at night in cold water; and so Magen Avraham implies — and this is astonishing, for also even without erev Yom Tov it is permitted in cold water on the seventh day of mourning even by day, as Shach wrote siman 381; and in truth it is no difficulty from siman 511, for in such a case there it is permitted even in hot water; one may also say Rama informs us: since there is no prohibition of hot bathing on Yom Tov only out of stringency, etc. — see there at length.
eliyah-rabbah/10:_: [10] Even if he encountered him, etc. — and if they rebuked him even on the thirtieth day it is permitted; and see siman 541. She'eirei Knesset HaGedolah wrote on what the Tur wrote, 'however the Semak wrote,' etc. — this is his language; and likewise he wrote in Yoreh De'ah siman 375 — it implies this is his view; and one may wonder how he ruled without comment contrary to the Rosh who forbids, and likewise ruled in Shulchan Aruch; and one may wonder more about Beit Yosef who did not protest at all — up to here his language; and one may wonder at his wonder, for in Yoreh De'ah siman 375 the Tur rules like the Rosh; also I overlooked Beit Chadash siman 399 who wrote the Tur rules like the Rosh and did not write 'however the Semak wrote,' etc., but practiced leniently like him so as not to change from their custom; and with this I am satisfied with Bedek HaBayis's difficulty on Beit Yosef regarding the Tur — examine well, for I abbreviated since for practical law we follow Shulchan Aruch.
eliyah-rabbah/11:_: [11] After prayers, etc. This means that one must pray a mencha first, then the sanctity of the leg applies to him, and on the contrary, those who do not honor the leg, but other mourning laws, such as sitting on the ground and taking off shoes, are practiced until it gets dark (Meghan Avraham).
eliyah-rabbah/12:_: [12] But to Didan, etc. Tima in the Yod 29, section 5, Rama wrote about and there is a permit near darkness and so they practice, and the clothing in the 18th and 16th and the Shoch and the shield of Avraham is dehaka to the law and there is a custom for the custom of honoring a good day. To bathe in broth, therefore, if one dies on the eve of Shabbat and that Shabbat is the eve of the pilgrimage, it is permissible to bathe on the eve of Shabbat as far as his language is concerned. And Tima Delkman wrote in 1915 that Rama's Damshum baptisms are permitted on the eve of Yom Kippur and on all other days of Yom Tov it is forbidden, so it seems to me that it is simple and clear that Rama's words in the Yod Hach Mili and Didan are forbidden, etc As Rama wrote, and this is how we used to be in the grave, they died seven days before the Domtar Hajj, close to the darkness of the first Deldea, it is forbidden until the night, as the Beit Yosef wrote there, and I also found in the Parishah there, one must also say my thoughts even during a Shava, and Kai about a cold wash in a Domtar after a Shava, look at what he wrote The Shachak pointed to Shafa and likewise it should be said in the washing in water only when the Nami after seven is written, as the Shachak wrote in the Shafta section 2, and it is not a kamer but it is customary to allow close to dark, but it is forbidden to wash in water and to wash with salt and buret. kaf-hachayyim/2:_: (2) There — mourning does not apply on the festival, for they are days of joy and "you shall rejoice in your festival" — communal positive mitzvah overrides individual mourning positive mitzvah, even day one which is Torah positive mitzvah — Levush; all the more per view that no mourning is d'oraisa even day one, only aninut, as Beit Yosef in name of Rosh — see there; see Yoreh De'ah 399:13 that the world holds like those who say no mourning is d'oraisa — see there; see below seif 2:
kaf-hachayyim/3:_: c) Name. It does not apply to him with mourning, etc., nor does it change his place, nor does it change, but he changes the foot of the mm who has not yet started mourning, one should not walk like that on foot. Maharam of Lublin C. 17. And so on above C. 157 O. 35 in the name of Maharai from Bruna Yaush. And this is per the Mish Moram Zal Bhaga in the Yod Sesi' that the Duff on Shabbat changes its place, but per the Mish Shem the Sha'a the practice is not to change their place on Shabbat in the Bechan, they do Yaush, in the Omnipresent there are no changes. And refer to MS in this, the Barchi, there, O. 2, Yaush:
kaf-hachayyim/4:_: (4) There. Mourning did not apply to him, etc. — but regarding lighting the candle of honor for the deceased, the festival does not cancel; and even when one died on the festival they light the candle. However, in a room where everyone eats there — even if the deceased died there — one should not light on Yom Tov lest through this he come to eulogy; and one should light it in the synagogue or in one of the rooms of the house where they do not eat. Responsum Noda B'Yehuda siman 73. Avnei Nezer in siman 533 end section 7 — Sha'arei Teshuvah section 1, Mishna Berurah section 3; and when he does not light it in the synagogue or in a place where they eat there on Yom Tov, one should light it through a non-Jew. Maharsham siman 532; and see above siman 514 section 79 and below end section 32.
kaf-hachayyim/5:_: (5) There — and counts thirty from burial day, etc.; Shulchan Aruch counts in place of seven and completes thirty as seif 16. R' Shlomo responsum 5, Mishna Berurah 71, Darkei Moshe Yoreh De'ah 399 letter 2; so Shach there s.k. 7. However in Hagahot Maimoniyot chapter 10 wrote: specifically when buried before Sukkot — Shmini Atzeret counts for seven as below seif 16; unlike here buried during festival — only one day counts — see there; Beit David, Beit Yosef Yoreh De'ah 399; so Shulchan Aruch there seif 2; Levush; Bach; Taz there s.k. 4 and this siman s.k. 4, wrote unlike R' Shlomo and Mishna Berurah who followed him — see there; so Magen Avraham s.k. 1; Or Sameach 13; letter 11 Hagahot Tashbetz; Beit David siman 314 wrote such should be practiced, do not say halacha follows the lenient here — see there; so in his book Yosef Ometz 93:2; Bigdei Yesha agreed with Taz — see there; Chayei Adam general rule 169:2, Mishna Berurah 4; nevertheless Chayei Adam wrote since some say Shmini Atzeret counts for seven one may be lenient where he suffers, etc., for bathing and women — see there; per Mordechai z"l Yoreh De'ah 481:1 in gloss they practice nowadays to forbid all bathing all thirty days; but by law otherwise permitted after seven — see there; if so where they did not practice per Mordechai, after seven bathing is permitted; see below letter 37:
kaf-hachayyim/6:_: f) Name. as much as thirty. That is, shaving and getting a haircut and bathing in broth and other things that are explained in the Yod in the the Master Avilot Yaosh:
kaf-hachayyim/7:_: (7) [Seif 2] He counts the seven from the last second day of Yom Tov, etc. — and likewise on the second day of Yom Tov of Rosh Hashana; for example, if his deceased died on the first day of Yom Tov of Rosh Hashana, he counts the seven from the second day of Yom Tov, which is also from their words — Beit Chadash in Yoreh De'ah siman 399, Shach there s.k. 8. However, Taz there s.k. 7 distinguishes: specifically when buried on the second day of Rosh Hashana it counts for him, but buried on the first day the second day does not count for him, see there. And likewise in this siman s.k. 1; and likewise Mabit part 2 siman 89. Perach Mateh Aharon part 1 siman 98. However, Magen Avraham s.k. 2 wrote one should be lenient like Beit Chadash and his colleagues, see there. And likewise Avnei Nezer section 2; and likewise in Toras Chesed siman 4 and in Ginzei Yosef Chayei Adam general rule 5 siman 7 they agreed to the halakha like Beit Chadash, see there; and likewise agreed Beit Din siman 313. Sha'arei Teshuvah section 3, Yeshuos Yaakov section 3, Mateh Yehuda in his book Shevet Yehuda on Yoreh De'ah siman 399 wrote and so they practice. And likewise testified Maharam of Amstelveen that so was done in practice in the rabbinical court of the rabbi Perach Magen Avraham. And Beit Din in the book Torach Chaim part 3 in the book Olelos HaKerem siman 11. Section 11 in Hagahot Beit Yosef on Rosh Hashana section 1, Nahar Shalom section 2, Chochmas Adam general rule 169 section 2, Mishna Berurah section 8.

kaf-hachayyim/17:_: (17) There — private matters apply; some say even private matters do not apply on the festival — Beit Yosef in name of Rambam; so Rashdam Chiddushei De'ot siman 202; Beit David Knesset HaGedolah in Hagahot Beit Yosef; but Shulchan Aruch ruled like most poskim that even on the festival private matters apply as Beit Yosef — see there; private matters are: shoes, bathing, Torah study as Yoreh De'ah siman 400 — see there; also some things called public — see there. Ateret Zekenim letter 3 to be lenient in Torah study on festival per view in Tur Yoreh De'ah 400 that study is public; although we do not rule so, nevertheless on festival one may rely on poskim who hold one does not practice even private matters — see there; so responsum Chacham Tzvi 100 to be lenient in study on festival — see there; Beit David Shaarei Teshuvah letter 5: if so obvious he may review Moed Katan chapter even if no obligation (as siman 285) — not worse than other study permitted — see there; nevertheless to read Torah on festival to count him among readers — l'chatchila not proper, Mishna Berurah 16:

shaarei-teshuvah/5:_: In private — Or Sameach; it implies from Magen Avraham that even Torah study is permitted only for bad matters; Chacham Tzvi 100 wrote he ruled for a scholar accustomed to review Mishnayot by heart — permitted to review all the festival, even though private matters apply; nevertheless permitted: one, no greater loss than forgetting if he does not review; we do not find permission for loss except in what is not actual joy; further, specifically other years when he could engage in Jeremiah, etc.; on festival improper to engage in this and improper to sit idle from Torah; also Rambam holds on festival one does not practice even private matters; see Yoreh De'ah 399 Tur and Beit Yosef — Rambam is not alone; therefore even without loss in memorized Mishnayot one may rely on Rambam and supporters to learn "all the ordinances of the Holy One, blessed be He, are upright," etc. — see there; if so obvious he may review Moed Katan chapter even without obligation — not worse than other permitted study — see there:
shaarei-teshuvah/6:_: (In Shulchan Aruch seif 8) and all the more so if his eighth day falls on erev Shabbat, etc. — and see in responsum Beit Chadash HaChadashot siman 12 that it is permitted to return immediately to his place at the entry of this Shabbat; and likewise permitted to wear Shabbat garments; nevertheless forbidden to enter the wedding hall on this Shabbat, see there; and likewise the view of Beit Hillel in Yoreh De'ah siman 399. But Shevut Yaakov part 1 siman 90 responded to Beit Chadash and his view is to forbid returning to his place and wearing Shabbat garments, see there; and he wrote there is no proof from the cancellation of his thirty on Shabbat that is permitted on erev Shabbat — there the Rama is lenient that one may say the 29th day is like a weekday, etc., as appears from Darkei Moshe siman 10, see there; and nevertheless it appears since Beit Chadash permits this, which is only the custom of instructors to be lenient, it is not an error in ruling, as Shevut Yaakov wrote he has what to rely on from what Darkei Moshe wrote — there is no proof from that; for perhaps even though it is impossible on Shabbat, therefore he needed to combine the matter that one may say regarding bathing that is forbidden by law — one might think to forbid, for the 29th day is like the view that, etc.; but changing place and wearing Shabbat garments, which are only custom, are permitted; and perhaps if Shevut Yaakov saw Beit Chadash's words he would retract his view and rule halakha like Beit Hillel. In any case, regarding wearing Shabbat garments it seems to be stringent if they are new and their pressing is still very evident — see Yoreh De'ah siman 389 seif 5 and below in Magen Avraham siman 551 s.k. 30; and if he has no others, perhaps there is room to be lenient even in this.
